# On Learning to Ride Your Brain

Wrote a longer [substack version](https://contraptions.venkateshrao.com/p/on-learning-to-ride-your-brain)

Steve Jobs was wrong. A traditional computer was never a bicycle for the brain. It was never a coherent enough machine to require, or enable, the holistic mode of dynamically stabilized control that is “riding a bike” after learning to “balance” it. At best, a traditional computer is like a set of power tools. If urs an Apple, it’s a coherently branded set of power tools in a nice toolbox, but not an integrated machine.

AI has revealed this by revealing itself to be a *motorcycle* for the brain. See the thing is, the brain *itself* is a combination rider+bicycle type entity. The “bicycle” part is loosely “intelligence” and the “rider” part is the part that has *learned* how to manage attention, a process that is strikingly similar to learning to ride a bike. To understand how this works, we have to dig pretty deep into the sociology of how “smart” is constructed and socialized in human society in two ways.

Unless you’re active in one of the domains where savant performance is meaningful, like chess, music, or number theory, “smart” tends to be highly socially constructed as some mix of academic performance, extracurricular depth, and social presentation. Good grades, evidence of depth outside of textbooks, and most importantly, a capacity for lively social interaction that subtly dominates conversation by topping others’ arguments, citing deeper knowledge sources, and referencing the right hooks into relevant authoritative discourses. Generally this amounts to an ongoing demonstration that almost any subject is deeper and more complex than the casual dilettante appreciates.

The “smart” person is basically living proof of the shallowness of the mental life of the median person on the median topic, who is revealed to be, not stupid per se, but unaware of the meta of most topics they weigh in on. Curiously, logic and reason play almost no role in the performance of smartness, since smartness typically operates by subverting the lazy presumption that you’re operating with the right terms of reference to even begin applying logic and reason.

Smartness operates by vividly demonstrating the conversational incompetence of the interlocutor, with varying degrees of grace and kindness, to *their* satisfaction, cowing them into suitable deference or demonstrating them to be crackpots in denial. This model of smarts is what’s performed by Matt Damon in the Good Will Hunting bar scene (not the math scenes). Real-life examples are less dramatically intense, but this how people are “normally” judged to be “smart.” Thats why interviews are a gatekeeping mechanism. They are stylized versions of a normal social process.

Three pathological “smartness” cultures derive from this basic smartness culture via degeneracy and fail to function the same way. There are 3 basic degeberacies:

1. Virtuoso IQ performances on inadequately persuasive ontological ground. This separates the audience into future acolytes and skeptics who tag you as a solipsistic egghead with an unconvincing halo, who doesn’t realize they’re prematurely trying to “reason” without establishing common grounds and motives for it. Cults start this way.
1. Overdeveloped “debate” “or “wit” skills that dazzle without persuading, by relying on tactical speed. Political and legal theaters start this way.
1. Demonstrations of deep erudition that turn conversations into tedious lectures that presume the authority of a tradition rather than establishing it. Ivory towers start this way.

All three modes create escaped realities that are only persuasive if you are inside them. They create diverging dissensus realities. By contrast, “normal” smartness performances are *generally* persuasive. The create converging consensus realities. Which one dominates determines whether narratives are overall convergent or divergent.

But none of this is actually that interesting. Performative smartness behaviors, both normie and degenerate, constitute a kind of consensus social proof process layer of society. Sociological intelligence that underwrites societal governance but has a very vague relationship with the truth at best. It’s what we are socialized into. Like getting a driving license. I recall when I was first tagged “smart” beyond my immediate family, sometime in 5th grade, with firm membership achieved by the 8th grade. There was real signal there, but not in the visible signals.

The real signal was that between 5th and 8th grades, I learned to actually manage my attention and direct it where I wanted. “This is thinkable and I can think about it by just paying steady attention, which I can do” became a basic move for me. I started coming across as “generally smart” to others as a side effect. I was officially “licensed to smart.”

The thing about this is, it actually has nothing to do with any notion of intelligence. *That* is much more like learning to ride a bike, which revealingly *does not* have or require a licensing regime unlike car driving. Your balancing circuits visibly cross a threshold. You’re *visibly oriented* as a human+bike system in the one case, and as a “generative brain +attention regulation system” in the other. You may still need to learn some safe riding behaviors for traffic, but nobody demands to see your biking license once you demonstrate you can ride. By contrast it’s possible to fake being able to drive a car safely, which is why licenses are needed.

The bike-riding quality of attention management becomes clearer in adulthood when you start to notice people you thought were “stupid” suddenly turning “on” and becoming seriously impressive in some way. They’ve learned to balance on their brain bikes. Their attention is controlled, directable, coherent and steady. At least some of the time. Sometimes it presents as “general intelligence” and other times it presents as other traits, like drive, imagination, betting acumen, foresight, attunement, relentlessness, agility.

*Absence* of this capacity becomes equally noticeable. Sometimes this can even lead to question marks on previous assessment of “smart.” Some notations on your “license to smart” like “ADHD” or “OCD” tag *qualifued* attention control (“this person can be trusted to ride their brain bike without falling off or failing to steer under these condition”). Others come across as some sort of undiagnosed tragic failure.

It’s only when you’ve come to terms with such phenomenology that you realize that “smart” is just an early, narrow legibilization of *one* way mastery of attention (and more generally, regulation of emotions and psyche) can manifest early, in teenagers. It’s not perfect mastery. Knowing how to ride a bike doesn’t mean you’ll never fall off, or be able to stay in control under all conditions. 

But there’s a clear and sharp observable point where someone visibly masters balance. They’ve driven a “balancing protocol” into the unconscious brain stem later. And this is visible with both bike-riding and attention-governing. And in both cases, there are people who somehow seem to never get there. With bicycles at least there’s a clear reason why — you need a bike and some concentrated learning effort, and a culture that makes that a routine part of growing up, to the point that we’re surprised when an adult admits they never learned to ride a bike. We’re surprised but don’t think the worse of them for it, because we correctly presume that it’s something almost anyone can learn (modulo some neurological conditions).

But learning to “ride your brain” is not really a thing society solves for directly.

Why am I going on about this? Because “intelligence” in practice is not the social performance associated with “license to smart” but the demonstrated capability to “ride your brain” in some visible way.

This brings us to AI. AI is like riding a powered two-wheeler, like a motorcycle or scooter. Some people who learn to ride a bike never go on to learn to ride powered two-wheelers. You need *excess* regulatory capacity to manage the greater mass and velocity. This is *harder* than either riding a bike or driving a car.

A lot of failure to use AI effectively looks to me like bike riders struggling with two wheelers because they have acquired licenses to drive 4-wheelers.

So to adopt AI you really need to have an overdeveloped capacity to ride your own brain. With sufficient surplus supervisory capacity to balance the “motorcycle.” To extend the metaphor, the motorcycle can become self-balancing, but though we’re already there with robot motorcycles, we’re not yet there with brain motorcycles. Most (but not all) safety failures and risks amount to an insufficiently skilled bicycle rider getting thrown off the motorcycle, which then proceeds to get unbalanced and crash in some way.

changelog.note: Added a new opening that disputes Jobs's "bicycle for the mind" idea, casting traditional computers as power tools and AI as the brain's motorcycle. The rest of the essay is unchanged.

Extended the closing with a few new sentences: the motorcycle metaphor now covers self-balancing, with robot motorcycles contrasted with brain ones, and most AI safety failures are framed as underskilled riders being thrown off.
Added a line at the top linking to a longer Substack version of the essay. The body text is unchanged.
